fixes.explanation: A garden would be a lovely thing to have, but it isn't in this verse. Solomon, David's son and Israel's king, planned a house for the Name of the LORD and a royal palace for himself. Palace is the word that fits the blank.

Silver comes up later in Solomon's message, where he asks Hiram, king of Tyre, for a craftsman skilled in working with it. But in this verse Solomon is talking about what Hiram once did for his father David. Hiram sent David cedars to build himself a house to live in. Solomon wants that same help again.

Solomon, David's son and Israel's king, tells Hiram the burnt offerings will be made every morning and evening. They'll also be made on the Sabbaths, New Moons and appointed feasts of the LORD. That's a steady rhythm, twice a day.

Bethel isn't named in this verse. Solomon, David's son and Israel's king, says the craftsman from Tyre will work with his craftsmen in Judah and Jerusalem. His father David provided those craftsmen. Jerusalem is the one that fits the blank.

Hebron didn't make the guest list for this verse, friend. Solomon, David's son and Israel's king, says the craftsman from Tyre will work with his own craftsmen in Judah and Jerusalem. Those are the craftsmen his father David provided. Jerusalem is what goes in the blank.

Hiram, king of Tyre, writes, "Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who made the heavens and the earth! He has given King David a wise son with insight and understanding…" That wise son is Solomon, who is getting the letter. Hiram put it in writing, friend. That's a nice thing to find in the mail.

Hiram, king of Tyre, says Huram-abi, the craftsman he's sending, is "…the son of a woman from the daughters of Dan…" His father is a man of Tyre. So his mother comes from the daughters of Dan, and his father is from Tyre.

Judah shows up in this passage, so I see why it caught your eye. But Hiram, king of Tyre, says Huram-abi, the craftsman he's sending, is the son of a woman from the daughters of Dan. His father is a man of Tyre. Dan is the one that fits.

Levi's a fine name, but it didn't make it into Hiram's letter. Hiram, king of Tyre, says Huram-abi, the craftsman he's sending, is the son of a woman from the daughters of Dan. His father is a man of Tyre. So the answer is Dan, friend.

Hiram, king of Tyre, says, "We will cut logs from Lebanon, as many as you need, and we will float them to you as rafts by sea down to Joppa." So the logs ride the water instead of a road. I think that beats carrying them one at a time. Solomon can take them up to Jerusalem from there.

Carts aren't in Hiram's plan. Hiram, king of Tyre, says his men will cut the logs in Lebanon and float them as rafts by sea. They're headed down to Joppa. After that, Solomon can take them up to Jerusalem.

Camels don't show up in Hiram's letter. Hiram, king of Tyre, says, "…we will float them to you as rafts by sea down to Joppa." The sea does the hauling. After that, Solomon can take the logs up to Jerusalem.
Tarshish isn't in Hiram's letter. Hiram, king of Tyre, says the log rafts will float by sea down to Joppa. After that, Solomon can take the logs up to Jerusalem. Joppa is the port in this plan.
